stem: You start a container with `docker run -d nginx` and pass no `--network` flag. Which network is it attached to on Docker Engine for Linux?

options.text: The default `bridge` network
options.why: Containers started without `--network` join the built-in default bridge network.

options.text: The `host` network
options.why: Host networking is opt-in with `--network host`; it is never the default.

options.text: A new user-defined bridge named after the container
options.why: Docker does not create a network per container; Compose creates per-project networks, plain `docker run` does not.

options.text: No network at all, until you publish a port
options.why: Containers have networking enabled by default and can make outgoing connections even with nothing published.

explanation: When Docker Engine starts on Linux it creates three networks: `bridge` (the default bridge, `docker0`), `host` and `none`. A container started without `--network` is connected to the default bridge. The docs call that network a legacy detail that is not recommended for production; use a user-defined bridge instead.

stem: Two containers, `web` and `db`, are both started on the default `bridge` network without any extra flags. From inside `web`, the hostname `db` resolves to the `db` container's IP address.

options.text: True
options.why: Name resolution between containers is a feature of user-defined networks, not of the default bridge.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: containers on the default bridge can only reach each other by IP address unless you use the legacy `--link` flag.

explanation: Automatic DNS resolution by container name or alias is provided only on user-defined networks, through Docker's embedded DNS server. On the default bridge, containers get a copy of the host's `/etc/resolv.conf` and can reach each other only by IP, or with the legacy `--link` flag. Creating a user-defined bridge and attaching both containers to it is the fix.

stem: Containers attached to a user-defined network use Docker's embedded DNS server, which forwards external lookups to the host's DNS servers. Type its IPv4 address as seen from inside the container.
explanation: The embedded DNS server listens on `127.0.0.11` inside every container on a user-defined network. It answers container names and network aliases, and forwards everything else to the DNS servers configured on the host. There is no IPv6 equivalent; the IPv4 address works even in IPv6-only containers.

stem: Match each Docker network driver to the situation it fits best.

options.text: `bridge` (user-defined)
options.why: Single-host networking with name resolution and isolation.

options.text: `host`
options.why: Shares the host's network namespace; no NAT and no per-container IP.

options.text: `none`
options.why: Only a loopback interface; full network isolation.

options.text: `overlay`
options.why: Spans several Docker hosts joined in a swarm.

options.text: `macvlan`
options.why: Gives the container its own MAC address on the physical network.

prompts.text: Several containers on one host must talk to each other by name
A latency-sensitive service that listens on hundreds of ports and should avoid NAT
A batch job that processes local files and must have no network access at all
Services on three different Docker hosts need one shared network
A legacy app must appear as a physical device with its own MAC address on the LAN

explanation: User-defined bridges are the default choice on one host: they add DNS by name and isolate unrelated stacks. `host` removes network isolation and NAT, which helps when a container handles many ports. `none` leaves only a loopback device. `overlay` builds a distributed network across swarm nodes. `macvlan` assigns a MAC address so the container looks like a physical device on the network.

stem: What does `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx` do?

options.text: Maps container port 8080 to host port 80
options.why: The order is `host:container`, so this reverses the mapping.

options.text: Maps host port 8080 to container port 80
options.why: The first number is the host port and the second is the container port.

options.text: Exposes port 80 to other containers only
options.why: Publishing makes the port reachable from outside the host, not just from other containers.

options.text: Forwards UDP port 8080 to container port 80
options.why: Without a `/udp` suffix the mapping is TCP only.

explanation: The `-p` (`--publish`) flag takes `[host-ip:]host-port:container-port[/protocol]`. `-p 8080:80` maps TCP port 8080 on every host address to TCP port 80 in the container. Add `/udp` for UDP, and add an IP such as `127.0.0.1:` in front to limit which host address listens.
reference: Docker docs: Port publishing and mapping

stem: A container is started with `--network none`. Which network interfaces does it have?

options.text: A loopback device and one `eth0` with no gateway
options.why: With `none`, Docker creates no `eth0` at all.

options.text: No interfaces of any kind
options.why: The loopback device is still created inside the container.

options.text: Only the loopback device
options.why: The `none` driver isolates the network stack, leaving just `lo`.

options.text: The same interfaces as the host
options.why: Sharing the host's interfaces is what `--network host` does.

explanation: The `none` driver completely isolates a container's networking: only the loopback device is created. It suits workloads that must not reach the network at all. Note that no IPv6 loopback address is configured for containers using the `none` driver.

stem: A Dockerfile contains `EXPOSE 3000`. Running the image with a plain `docker run myimage` makes port 3000 reachable from other machines on the network.

options.text: True
options.why: `EXPOSE` records metadata about which port the app uses; it does not create any host mapping.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `EXPOSE` only documents the port; nothing is published until you use `-p` or `-P`.

explanation: `EXPOSE` (or `--expose`) marks a port as exposed without publishing it to the host. To make it reachable from outside, publish it with `-p host:container`, or use `-P` to publish every exposed port to a random host port.
reference: Docker docs: docker container run reference

stem: Which two are advantages of a user-defined bridge network over the default `bridge` network? (Choose two.)

options.text: Containers can resolve each other by name or alias
options.why: User-defined networks use the embedded DNS server, so names work without `--link`.

options.text: Only containers attached to that network can talk to each other
options.why: It scopes communication, unlike the shared default bridge every unattached container joins.

options.text: Containers on it share the host's IP address and ports
options.why: That describes the `host` driver, not a bridge.

options.text: Published ports are reachable only from the host itself
options.why: Published ports bind to all host addresses by default on any bridge.

options.text: Containers keep the same IP address after they are recreated
options.why: IP addresses are allocated dynamically; names, not IPs, are the stable handle.

explanation: User-defined bridges provide automatic DNS resolution between containers and better isolation: every container started without `--network` lands on the default bridge, so unrelated stacks can reach each other there. User-defined networks also let you connect and disconnect running containers on the fly.

stem:
An API container logs `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND db`. Both containers were started like this:

```bash
docker run -d --name db postgres:17
docker run -d --name api -e DATABASE_HOST=db myapi
```

What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Add `--link db` to the api container and keep the default bridge
options.why: It works, but `--link` is legacy and must be wired in both directions as stacks grow.

options.text: Set `DATABASE_HOST` to the db container's current IP address
options.why: Container IPs change when containers are recreated, so this breaks on the next restart.

options.text: Create a user-defined network and start both containers on it
options.why: User-defined networks give containers DNS resolution by name through the embedded DNS server.

options.text: Publish the db port with `-p 5432:5432` and use `localhost`
options.why: `localhost` inside the api container is the api container itself, not the host.

explanation: Both containers are on the default bridge, where names don't resolve. Create a network (`docker network create appnet`) and run both with `--network appnet`, or attach existing ones with `docker network connect appnet db`. The api can then reach `db:5432` without publishing anything to the host.

stem: A Node.js container and a Postgres container are on the same user-defined network. Postgres is published with `-p 5432:5432`. From inside the Node container, `psql -h localhost -p 5432` fails with "connection refused". Why?

options.text: Inside a container, `localhost` is the container's own loopback, not the host or the db
options.why: Each container has its own network namespace and loopback device.

options.text: Published ports are only reachable from other hosts, not from containers
options.why: Published ports are reachable from containers too, but via the host, not via `localhost`.

options.text: Postgres refuses connections from other containers until you set `listen_addresses` to `localhost`
options.why: Setting `listen_addresses` to localhost would block other containers, not allow them.

options.text: The embedded DNS server rewrites `localhost` to `127.0.0.11`
options.why: The embedded DNS server never rewrites `localhost`; that name resolves from `/etc/hosts`.

explanation: Every container has its own network namespace, so `localhost` means the container itself. Connect to the database by its container name (`psql -h db`) on the shared network; publishing 5432 isn't needed for container-to-container traffic at all.

stem: A Flask app runs `app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000)` in a container started with `-p 5000:5000`. On the host, `curl localhost:5000` returns "connection reset by peer". What is the fix?

options.text: Publish with `-p 127.0.0.1:5000:5000` so both sides use loopback
options.why: The host side isn't the problem; the app inside still only listens on the container's loopback.

options.text: Add `EXPOSE 5000` to the Dockerfile
options.why: `EXPOSE` is documentation and changes nothing about where the app listens.

options.text: Run the container with `--network none`
options.why: That removes networking entirely, so nothing could reach the app.

options.text: Make the app listen on `0.0.0.0` inside the container
options.why: Forwarded traffic arrives on the container's `eth0`, which a loopback-only listener ignores.

explanation: Port publishing forwards traffic to the container's network interface (`eth0`), not to its loopback. A server bound to `127.0.0.1` inside the container accepts only connections that originate inside that same container. Bind to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) and keep the publish rule, optionally limiting the host side with `-p 127.0.0.1:5000:5000`.
reference: Docker docs: Port publishing and mapping

stem: An image declares `EXPOSE 80 443`. What does `docker run -d -P myimage` do?

options.text: Publishes container ports 80 and 443 on the same host ports
options.why: That mapping needs explicit `-p 80:80 -p 443:443`; `-P` picks host ports itself.

options.text: Publishes 80 and 443 to random high ports on the host
options.why: `-P` maps every exposed port to a random high port on the host.

options.text: Publishes every port the app opens at runtime
options.why: `-P` only uses ports declared with `EXPOSE` or `--expose`, not ports opened later.

options.text: Exposes the ports to other containers but not to the host
options.why: That's what `EXPOSE` alone does; `-P` actually publishes them.

explanation: `-P` (`--publish-all`) publishes every port that is explicitly exposed, via the Dockerfile `EXPOSE` instruction or the `--expose` flag, binding each one to a random port from the host's ephemeral range (`/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range`). Use `docker port <container>` to see which host ports were chosen.
reference: Docker docs: docker container run reference

stem: On Docker Engine for Linux, a container must call an API that runs directly on the host, listening on all interfaces at port 8000. Which two approaches work? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run with `--add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway` and call `host.docker.internal:8000`
options.why: The special `host-gateway` value resolves to the host's internal IP address.

options.text: Run the container with `--network host` and call `localhost:8000`
options.why: With host networking the container shares the host's namespace, so localhost is the host.

options.text: Call `localhost:8000` from a container on the default bridge
options.why: On a bridge, localhost is the container itself.

options.text: Call `127.0.0.11:8000` because that address belongs to the host
options.why: `127.0.0.11` is the embedded DNS server inside the container, not the host.

options.text: Call `host.docker.internal:8000` without any extra flag, exactly as on Docker Desktop
options.why: Docker Desktop resolves that name automatically; Docker Engine on Linux needs `--add-host`.

explanation: The `--add-host` flag supports a special `host-gateway` value that resolves to the host's internal IP address, and the convention is to name it `host.docker.internal`. Docker Desktop adds that name automatically, but on Linux you add it yourself. Host networking also works, at the cost of losing network isolation.
reference: Docker docs: docker container run reference

stem: You containerize a DNS server that must answer queries over both UDP and TCP on port 53. Which publish flags are correct?

options.text: `-p 53:53`, which covers both protocols
options.why: Without a protocol suffix this publishes TCP only, so normal UDP queries fail.

options.text: `-p 53:53/udp`, since DNS only uses UDP
options.why: That covers UDP but not TCP, which DNS needs for large responses and zone transfers.
Each protocol needs its own mapping.

options.text: `-p 53:53/tcp+udp` in a single flag
options.why: There is no `any` protocol suffix; use one `-p` per protocol.

explanation: A publish rule maps one protocol. `-p 8080:80` is TCP, `-p 8080:80/udp` is UDP, and you combine both with two flags: `-p 53:53/tcp -p 53:53/udp`.
reference: Docker docs: Port publishing and mapping

stem: A container is started with `docker run --network host -p 8080:80 nginx` on Linux. What happens?

options.text: nginx is reachable on host port 8080, forwarded to its port 80
options.why: Port mapping does not take effect in host mode.

options.text: The command fails because `-p` conflicts with `--network host`
options.why: Docker doesn't fail; it starts the container and prints a warning.

options.text: nginx gets its own IP address, and port 80 is published on it
options.why: In host mode the container has no IP address of its own.

options.text: Ports are ignored with a warning; nginx uses host port 80
options.why: The container shares the host's network stack, so its port 80 is the host's port 80.

explanation: With the `host` driver the container shares the host's network namespace and gets no IP address of its own, so `-p`, `--publish`, `-P` and `--publish-all` are ignored with the warning "Published ports are discarded when using host network mode". The app is reachable on whatever port it binds, here 80 on the host.

stem: Complete the command so the running container `pg17` can also be reached as `db` on the network `appnet`: `docker network connect --____ db appnet pg17`. Type the option name without dashes.
explanation: `--alias` adds a network-scoped alias: other containers on `appnet` can resolve `db` to `pg17`, and you can pass it several times (`--alias db --alias postgres`). Aliases apply only on the network where you set them.

stem: Two running containers, `api` and `cache`, are on the default bridge. You want `api` to reach `cache` by name without recreating either container. Put the steps in order.

options.text: Run `docker network create backend`
options.why: You need a user-defined network before you can attach anything to it.

options.text: Run `docker network connect backend cache`
options.why: Attach the target container to the new network.

options.text: Run `docker network connect backend api`
options.why: Attach the client container as well, so both share the network.

options.text: Test with `docker exec api getent hosts cache`
options.why: Resolution only works once both containers are on the same user-defined network.

explanation: Running containers can be attached to and detached from user-defined networks on the fly with `docker network connect` and `docker network disconnect`. Once both are on `backend`, the embedded DNS server resolves `cache`. The two connect steps can run in either order, but both must happen before the name will resolve.

stem: Container A is on user-defined bridge `net1` and container B is on user-defined bridge `net2`, on the same host with default settings. A can reach B on B's container IP address and any port.

options.text: True
options.why: Bridges are isolated from each other by default; only ports published to the host are reachable across networks.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Docker installs rules so containers on different bridge networks can only communicate through published ports.

explanation: The bridge driver installs firewall rules so that containers on different bridge networks can communicate only through published ports. To let A talk to B directly, connect one of them to both networks.

stem: Which command shows the containers attached to the network `appnet`, along with each one's IP address on that network?

options.text: `docker network ls`
options.why: It lists networks and their drivers, not the containers attached to them.

options.text: `docker port appnet`
options.why: `docker port` takes a container and lists its published ports.

options.text: `docker network inspect appnet`
options.why: Its `Containers` section lists each attached container with its IPv4/IPv6 address.

options.text: `docker ps --filter network=appnet --format "{{.Ports}}"`
options.why: The filter is real, but this prints published ports, not each container's network IP.

explanation: `docker network inspect <network>` returns the network's subnet, gateway and options, plus a `Containers` map with each attached container's name, MAC address and IP addresses. Pair it with `docker inspect <container>` to see a container's view of all its networks.

stem: On an Ubuntu server, `ufw` is enabled with only port 22 allowed. You run `docker run -d -p 5432:5432 postgres`. A security scan reports 5432 open to the internet. Why?

options.text: ufw allows every port above 1024 by default on Ubuntu
options.why: ufw's default is deny incoming; the port range has nothing to do with it.

options.text: Docker's NAT diverts it before ufw's INPUT rules
options.why: Published traffic is DNAT-ed and forwarded, so it never passes ufw's INPUT chain.

options.text: Postgres opens the port with raw sockets, bypassing iptables
options.why: Postgres uses normal sockets; Docker's rules are what publish the port.

options.text: ufw ignores ports opened after it was enabled
options.why: ufw rules apply to new traffic regardless of when a listener started.

explanation: Docker and ufw are incompatible by design. Docker routes container traffic in the `nat` table, so packets to a published port are diverted before they reach the INPUT and OUTPUT chains that ufw uses. Publish only to loopback (`-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432`), don't publish at all and use a Docker network, or filter in the `DOCKER-USER` chain.
reference: Docker docs: Packet filtering and firewalls

stem: Continuing from a server where Docker-published ports bypass `ufw`: which two changes actually stop remote hosts from reaching the published Postgres port? (Choose two.)

options.text: Publish with `-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432` so only the host can connect
options.why: Binding the published port to loopback limits access to the Docker host itself (Docker Engine 28+).

options.text: Add a filtering rule to the `DOCKER-USER` chain
options.why: `DOCKER-USER` is evaluated before Docker's own forwarding rules.

options.text: Run `ufw deny 5432` and reload ufw
options.why: ufw's rules sit in chains the diverted traffic never reaches.

options.text: Append a DROP rule to the end of the FORWARD chain
options.why: Rules appended to FORWARD run after Docker's jumps have already accepted the packet.

options.text: Add `EXPOSE 5432` to the Postgres image
options.why: `EXPOSE` is metadata and has no effect on firewalling.

explanation: Two documented options are to limit the host side of the mapping to `127.0.0.1` (or `::1`), and to put custom filters in `DOCKER-USER`, which Docker processes before `DOCKER-FORWARD` and `DOCKER`. Before Engine 28.0.0, hosts on the same L2 segment could still reach ports published to localhost, so upgrade too.
reference: Docker docs: Packet filtering and firewalls

stem: An admin runs `iptables -A FORWARD -s 203.0.113.0/24 -j DROP` to block a subnet from a container's published port, but the subnet can still connect. Why?

options.text: iptables rules don't apply to Docker traffic, which Docker routes through nftables only
options.why: Docker uses iptables by default; nftables is an optional backend.

options.text: The rule needs `-j REJECT`, because Docker ignores DROP targets
options.why: Docker has no special handling of DROP versus REJECT.

options.text: Docker's jump rules come earlier in FORWARD and accept the packet first
options.why: Appended rules run after Docker's chains; put the rule in `DOCKER-USER`.

options.text: FORWARD rules only apply to IPv6 traffic
options.why: FORWARD applies to forwarded IPv4 traffic; `ip6tables` handles IPv6.

explanation: Docker adds rules to FORWARD that unconditionally jump to `DOCKER-USER`, `DOCKER-FORWARD` and `DOCKER-INGRESS`. A packet accepted or rejected in those chains is never seen by rules appended later. Insert the rule into `DOCKER-USER` instead, for example `iptables -I DOCKER-USER -s 203.0.113.0/24 -j DROP`.

stem: A container publishes `-p 8080:80`. An admin adds `iptables -I DOCKER-USER -p tcp --dport 8080 -s 198.51.100.7 -j DROP`, but 198.51.100.7 can still load the site. What is wrong?

options.text: By the time DOCKER-USER runs, the packet is DNAT-ed to port 80
options.why: The rule should match the container port, or use conntrack's original destination port.

options.text: DOCKER-USER only accepts ACCEPT rules, not DROP rules
options.why: DOCKER-USER exists precisely so you can add filtering rules, DROP included.

options.text: `-I` inserts at the end of the chain, after Docker's ACCEPT
options.why: `-I` inserts at the top of the chain; `-A` appends.

options.text: Source matching doesn't work because Docker masquerades incoming traffic
options.why: Masquerading applies to outgoing connections; the client's source address is preserved.

explanation: Rules in `DOCKER-USER` see packets after Destination NAT, so they can only match the container's internal IP and port (80 here). To match the original request, use the conntrack extension, for example `-m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8080`; the docs note it may cost some performance.

stem:
A metrics sidecar should share the network namespace of the `app` container. What happens with this command?

```bash
docker run -d --name metrics --network container:app -p 9090:9090 prom/statsd-exporter
```

options.text: Port 9090 is published on the host and forwarded into the shared namespace
options.why: Containers in `container:` mode can't publish ports of their own.

options.text: The sidecar gets its own IP on app's network, plus the published port
options.why: `container:` mode shares app's stack; the sidecar gets no separate IP.

options.text: Docker rejects it: publish ports on the container that owns the namespace
options.why: `--publish` is among the flags `container:` networking doesn't support.

options.text: It works only if `app` was started with `--network host`
options.why: Sharing a namespace works with any network mode the owner uses.

explanation: With `--network container:<name|id>` the new container joins another container's network stack: same interfaces, same IP, same loopback. Flags that would configure networking are not supported in that mode: `--add-host`, `--hostname`, `--dns`, `--dns-search`, `--dns-option`, `--mac-address`, `--publish`, `--publish-all` and `--expose`. Publish 9090 on `app` instead; the sidecar's listener is then reachable through it.

stem: Match each `docker network create` option to its effect.

options.text: `--internal`
options.why: No default route; traffic to other networks is dropped.

options.text: `--attachable` (overlay)
options.why: Lets standalone containers, not just Swarm services, join.

options.text: `-o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false`
options.why: Disables inter-container connectivity on the bridge.

options.text: `-o com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1450`
options.why: Sets the MTU of container interfaces on the network.

prompts.text: Backend containers must talk to each other but must never reach the internet
A one-off `docker run` debug container must join a Swarm overlay network
Containers on this bridge must not be able to talk to each other
The host sits on a VXLAN underlay with a smaller packet size than Ethernet's 1500 bytes

explanation: An `--internal` network gets no default route, and firewall rules drop traffic to or from other networks; containers on it can still talk to each other and to the gateway address. `--attachable` opens an overlay to standalone containers. The bridge option `enable_icc` toggles inter-container connectivity, and `com.docker.network.driver.mtu` sets the MTU for container interfaces.

stem: A web container must reach the internet and talk to an API container. The API must never reach the internet. Which design meets both requirements?

options.text: Put both on one user-defined bridge and block the API's egress with `--dns 0.0.0.0`
options.why: Breaking DNS doesn't stop the API from connecting to IP addresses directly.

options.text: API only on an `--internal` network; web on that plus a normal bridge
options.why: The internal network has no default route, while the web container keeps egress through its other network.

options.text: Run the API with `--network none` and publish its port to the web container
options.why: `none` has no interfaces, so nothing could reach the API at all.

options.text: Put both on the default bridge and remove the API's published ports
options.why: Unpublished containers on the default bridge can still make outgoing internet connections.

explanation: A container can join several networks, like a host with several Ethernet cables. The docs give exactly this example: a frontend on a bridge with external access, plus an `--internal` network to reach backends that don't need external access. The internal network has no default route, so the API has no egress.

stem: A container is attached to two networks, `public` and `lan`, and outbound traffic sometimes leaves through the wrong one after `docker network connect` runs. How do you make `public` always the default gateway?

options.text: Connect `public` last, because the last network connected becomes the default route
options.why: Docker picks the gateway itself and it can change when connections change; connection order isn't a contract.

options.text: Add a route inside the container with `ip route` in the entrypoint
options.why: Fragile and needs `NET_ADMIN`; Docker may change the route again when networks change.

options.text: Use `--dns` to point at a server on the `public` network
options.why: DNS servers don't decide which gateway packets use.

options.text: Set `gw-priority` for `public` higher than the other networks
options.why: The network with the highest gw-priority (default 0) provides the default gateway.

explanation: When a container has several networks, Docker selects the default gateway and may change it whenever connections change. To pin it, set a gateway priority: `docker run --network name=public,gw-priority=1 --network lan …`, or pass `--gw-priority` to `docker network connect`. The highest priority wins, and the default is 0.

stem: Docker creates a filter-table chain specifically so administrators can add their own rules that are processed before Docker's forwarding rules. Type its name.
explanation: Rules in `DOCKER-USER` are evaluated before the rules in `DOCKER-FORWARD` and `DOCKER`. Rules appended to FORWARD come after Docker's, so they never see packets Docker has already accepted. Remember that packets in `DOCKER-USER` are already DNAT-ed to the container's address and port.

stem: A container on a `macvlan` network gets an address on the office LAN and is reachable from every laptop, but `curl` from the Docker host itself to that address times out. Why?

options.text: macvlan containers need `-p` port publishing to be reachable from their own host
options.why: macvlan traffic isn't NAT-ed; publishing ports doesn't apply.

options.text: A kernel rule blocks macvlan children from reaching their parent
options.why: This is a known kernel restriction of macvlan.

options.text: The host's ufw blocks traffic to macvlan addresses by default
options.why: Docker creates no firewall rules for macvlan, and ufw isn't the cause here.

options.text: macvlan containers only accept traffic from other containers
options.why: Other LAN devices can reach it, as the laptops show.

explanation: Containers on a macvlan network can't communicate with the host directly, a restriction in the Linux kernel. If the host must reach them, also connect the containers to a bridge network, or create a macvlan interface on the host with the same parent and an IP in the Docker network's subnet. Note that Docker creates no firewall rules for macvlan, ipvlan or host networking.

stem: Which two statements about Docker overlay networks are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Standalone containers can join only if the network was created with `--attachable`
options.why: Without `--attachable`, only Swarm services can connect.

options.text: Hosts need 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp and 4789/udp open between them
options.why: Those carry the control plane, node gossip and VXLAN data traffic.

options.text: They work between any Docker hosts without initializing or joining a swarm
options.why: You need swarm mode even for standalone containers on an overlay.

options.text: Application traffic is always encrypted, with no performance cost
options.why: Encryption is opt-in (`--opt encrypted`) and has a non-negligible cost.

options.text: They are created by default when Docker Engine starts
options.why: Only `bridge`, `host` and `none` exist at startup; the ingress overlay appears when a swarm starts.

explanation: Overlay networks span several Docker hosts and require swarm mode, even for standalone containers. Participating hosts must allow 2377/tcp (control plane), 7946/tcp and udp (node communication) and 4789/udp (VXLAN data). `--opt encrypted` adds IPsec at the VXLAN level, which costs performance, so test it first.

stem: A cron container connects to `172.18.0.5:6379`, which was Redis's IP last week. After a host reboot it fails. Which two statements explain the problem and its fix? (Choose two.)

options.text: Container IPs are assigned dynamically, and stopped containers lose their IP addresses
options.why: There is no guarantee Redis gets the same address after a restart.

options.text: Use the container name (or a network alias) on a shared user-defined network
options.why: The embedded DNS server keeps names pointing at the current IP.

options.text: Publish Redis with `-p 6379:6379` so its IP stays fixed
options.why: Publishing maps a host port; it doesn't pin the container IP.

options.text: Run Redis with `--network host` so it keeps 172.18.0.5
options.why: Host mode gives the container no IP of its own.

options.text: Container IPs are permanent; the reboot corrupted Docker's IPAM store
options.why: Changing addresses is normal behaviour, not corruption.

explanation: The daemon allocates IP addresses dynamically from each network's subnet, and the docs note that stopped containers lose their IP addresses. Names are the stable handle: on a user-defined network, connect to `redis:6379`. If you truly need a fixed address, pass `--ip` on a user-defined network, but DNS names are the usual answer.

stem: On Docker Engine releases older than 28.0.0, a port published with `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` could be reached by other machines on the same L2 segment (for example, the same switch).

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the docs warn that before 28.0.0, hosts on the same L2 segment could reach ports published to localhost.

options.text: False
options.why: This was a documented issue (moby/moby#45610), fixed in Engine 28.0.0.

explanation: Binding the host side to `127.0.0.1` or `::1` is the documented way to keep a published port host-only. The docs add a warning that in releases older than 28.0.0, hosts on the same L2 segment could still reach ports published to localhost. Treat older engines as exposed and upgrade.
reference: Docker docs: Port publishing and mapping

stem: A dual-stack Linux host runs `docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx` on an IPv4-only bridge network with default daemon settings. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Only the host's IPv4 addresses listen on 8080, because the network is IPv4-only
options.why: With no host IP given, Docker publishes on both `0.0.0.0` and `[::]`.

options.text: The command fails because IPv6 is enabled on the host but missing on the network
options.why: Docker handles this case; nothing fails.

options.text: All IPv4 and IPv6 host addresses; IPv6 is proxied to the container's IPv4
options.why: With the userland proxy on (the default), host IPv6 ports map to the container's IPv4 address.

options.text: Port 8080 listens only on `127.0.0.1` until you set a host IP
options.why: The default bind address is all interfaces, not loopback.

explanation: Without a host address, Docker publishes to every host address, `0.0.0.0` and `[::]`, possibly exposing the port to the world. If the bridge network is IPv4-only and `--userland-proxy=true` (the default), ports on the host's IPv6 addresses are mapped to the container's IPv4 address.
reference: Docker docs: Port publishing and mapping

stem: A LAN router has a static route sending `172.20.0.0/16` to a Docker host, and a client tries `curl http://172.20.0.10:80` straight to a container's IP. The port is also published as `-p 8080:80`. An admin adds an ACCEPT rule for that client in `DOCKER-USER`, but the request still fails. Why?

options.text: DOCKER-USER rules need a daemon restart before they take effect
options.why: iptables rules take effect immediately.

options.text: The route should point at `docker0` rather than the host's LAN address
options.why: Changing the route doesn't change how the host filters directly routed packets.

options.text: Direct access only works for ports published with `-P`
options.why: `-P` vs `-p` doesn't affect direct routing to container IPs.

options.text: A raw PREROUTING rule drops direct routes before DOCKER-USER
options.why: Use `allow-direct-routing` or `trusted_host_interfaces` to allow it.

explanation: By default, remote hosts may reach a container only through a port published on a host address. Packets sent to the container's own IP are dropped by a rule in the raw table's PREROUTING chain, which runs before the filter table, so `DOCKER-USER` can't allow them. To permit direct routing to published ports, set the daemon option `allow-direct-routing` or the network option `com.docker.network.bridge.trusted_host_interfaces`, or use a routed gateway mode.

stem: An IPv6 bridge network is created with `-o com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=routed`, and a container runs with `-p '[::]:8080:80'`. How do IPv6 clients reach the web server?

options.text: At the container's IPv6 address, port 80; host port 8080 is unused
options.why: In routed mode there is no NAT, so the host port in the mapping is ignored.

options.text: At the host's IPv6 address on port 8080, NAT-ed to port 80 as usual
options.why: That's `nat` mode; `routed` mode doesn't create the host-port translation.

options.text: At both addresses: the host's IPv6 on 8080 and the container's IPv6 on 80
options.why: Routed mode only opens access to the container address; there is no host-port NAT.

options.text: They can't: routed mode only works with `--internal` networks
options.why: That restriction belongs to the `isolated` gateway mode, not `routed`.

explanation: In `routed` gateway mode no NAT is set up. Published ports are opened on the container's own address, and remote hosts must have a route to the container network. The host port in a `-p` mapping is not used; the host address only decides whether the mapping applies to IPv4 or IPv6. If you give a specific address or port, it has no effect and a warning is logged. The `isolated` mode is the one that requires `--internal`.
reference: Docker docs: Port publishing and mapping

stem: Which three flags are NOT supported for a container started with `--network container:app`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `--hostname`
options.why: Hostname is part of the shared stack's identity, owned by `app`.

options.text: `--dns`
options.why: DNS settings come from the container that owns the namespace.

options.text: `--publish`
options.why: Ports must be published on the owning container.

options.text: `--env`
options.why: Environment variables are process settings, unrelated to networking.

options.text: `--volume`
options.why: Mounts are filesystem settings and work in any network mode.

options.text: `--memory`
options.why: Resource limits apply per container, regardless of network mode.

explanation: Joining another container's network stack means networking is configured once, on the owner. The docs list the unsupported flags: `--add-host`, `--hostname`, `--dns`, `--dns-search`, `--dns-option`, `--mac-address`, `--publish`, `--publish-all` and `--expose`. Non-network options like environment variables, volumes and resource limits still work.

stem: A company runs split-horizon DNS with two internal resolvers. One returns NXDOMAIN for `api.internal`, the other returns an address. Containers on the default bridge, given both servers via `--dns`, resolve the name only some of the time; containers on a user-defined network fail consistently. What explains the difference?

options.text: User-defined networks query upstream servers in parallel and pick the fastest answer
options.why: It's the other way round: the embedded DNS server queries in order.

options.text: The default bridge caches NXDOMAIN answers for 30 seconds
options.why: Docker documents no such cache; the behaviour comes from the resolver library.

options.text: User-defined networks ignore `--dns` and always use `8.8.8.8`
options.why: `--dns` works on user-defined networks too; the embedded server forwards to it.

options.text: Embedded DNS stops at the first NXDOMAIN; default-bridge resolvers vary
options.why: Some resolver libraries query in parallel and take the first response, even NXDOMAIN.

explanation: On the default bridge, how multiple DNS servers are queried is up to the container's resolver library: some query in order, others in parallel and use the first response, even if it is NXDOMAIN, which gives flaky results. On a custom network, the embedded DNS server queries upstream servers in order and stops after a successful response or an NXDOMAIN, so if the first server says NXDOMAIN it fails consistently. Servers configured for split-horizon need to agree, or the right one must come first.

stem: A Linux host runs a local caching resolver (dnsmasq) on `127.0.0.1:53`. A container is started with `--dns 127.0.0.1` on a bridge network, and every lookup times out. Why?

options.text: dnsmasq rejects queries from Docker's subnet unless you add `--add-host`
options.why: `--add-host` edits `/etc/hosts`; it has nothing to do with dnsmasq's ACL.

options.text: There `127.0.0.1` is the container's own loopback, not the host's
options.why: DNS requests are sent from the container's network namespace.

options.text: Docker forbids loopback DNS servers and silently drops the flag
options.why: The flag is applied; it just points at the wrong loopback.

options.text: Port 53 must be published with `-p 53:53/udp` for the container to query it
options.why: Publishing exposes container ports to the host, not host services to containers.

explanation: The docs spell it out: DNS requests are forwarded from the container's network namespace, so `--dns=127.0.0.1` refers to the container's own loopback address. Make the host resolver listen on an address the container can reach, such as the bridge gateway, and point `--dns` there, or rely on Docker's defaults.

stem: A remote client connects to host port 8080, published with `-p 8080:80` on a bridge network using the iptables backend. Put the stages the request passes through on the host in order.

options.text: Destination NAT in the nat table rewrites host:8080 to container-IP:80
options.why: NAT happens first, as the packet enters the host.

options.text: The routing decision sends the packet to FORWARD, not INPUT
options.why: After DNAT the destination is the container, so it's forwarded.

options.text: FORWARD jumps to DOCKER-USER, where admin rules are evaluated
options.why: Docker's first jump from FORWARD is to DOCKER-USER.

options.text: DOCKER-FORWARD and DOCKER accept it based on the port mapping
options.why: Docker's own rules accept traffic for published ports.

options.text: The packet leaves through the bridge into the container's eth0
options.why: Finally it is delivered across the Linux bridge to the container.

explanation: The nat table's DOCKER chain performs DNAT as the packet arrives, so it is routed through FORWARD rather than INPUT. That is why host firewalls such as ufw, which work on INPUT, never see it. FORWARD jumps to `DOCKER-USER` first, then to `DOCKER-FORWARD` and on to `DOCKER`, which accepts traffic matching a port mapping, and the packet crosses the bridge to the container.

stem: On a cloud VM whose NIC has an MTU of 1450 because of VXLAN encapsulation, containers on a bridge can resolve names and fetch small pages, but large HTTPS downloads and some TLS handshakes hang. What is the targeted fix?

options.text: Switch the network to `--internal` so traffic avoids the 1450-byte NIC
options.why: Internal networks have no external route, so the downloads would fail completely.

options.text: Raise the containers' MTU to 9000 to fit larger packets
options.why: A larger container MTU makes oversized packets worse on a 1450-byte path.

options.text: Set the network MTU to 1450 with `com.docker.network.driver.mtu`
options.why: Container interfaces then send packets that fit the smaller path.

options.text: Use `--dns 8.8.8.8` because the hangs come from slow DNS
options.why: Names already resolve; the symptom points at packet size, not DNS.

explanation: Small packets fit and large ones are silently dropped: that classic symptom of an MTU mismatch shows up on overlay or VXLAN-based cloud networks. Set the MTU of container interfaces with the bridge driver option `com.docker.network.driver.mtu` (the daemon's `mtu` setting covers the default bridge), so containers never send frames larger than the underlay can carry.

stem: A user-defined bridge is created with `-o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false`. Containers `a` and `b` are both attached, and `b` publishes `-p 9000:9000`. What can `a` do?

options.text: Reach `b` directly on any port, because ICC only affects the default bridge
options.why: The option applies to the network it is set on, user-defined bridges included.

options.text: Not reach `b` directly, while outbound access still works
options.why: Disabling inter-container connectivity blocks container-to-container traffic on that bridge.

options.text: Reach `b` only by name, because ICC filters traffic by IP address
options.why: ICC isn't about names versus IPs; it blocks direct traffic between the containers.

options.text: Make no network connections at all, outbound included
options.why: ICC doesn't affect egress through the gateway.

explanation: `com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc` (the `--icc` daemon flag for the default bridge) controls inter-container connectivity on a bridge. With it off, containers on the same bridge can't talk to each other directly, but they keep normal outbound access. It suits multi-tenant setups where neighbouring containers must not see each other.

stem: A RHEL host runs firewalld with the `public` zone allowing only SSH. Docker publishes `-p 8443:443`, and the port is reachable from outside. Which documented Docker behaviour explains this?

options.text: firewalld can't filter published TCP ports above 1024 on RHEL
options.why: firewalld can filter any port; the issue is which zone Docker's traffic uses.

options.text: Docker stops and disables firewalld when the daemon starts up
options.why: Docker integrates with firewalld instead of disabling it.

options.text: Docker adds port 8443 to the `public` zone automatically at publish time
options.why: Docker doesn't edit your zones; it creates its own zone and policy.

options.text: Docker's own `docker` zone (ACCEPT) plus an any-zone forwarding policy
options.why: Published traffic is forwarded through Docker's zone, not judged by `public`.

explanation: With firewalld enabled, Docker creates a firewalld zone called `docker` with target ACCEPT and inserts its bridge interfaces such as `docker0`. It also creates a `docker-forwarding` policy that allows forwarding from ANY zone to the `docker` zone. Published traffic is DNAT-ed and forwarded, so the `public` zone's rules don't block it. Restrict exposure at publish time or with `DOCKER-USER`.
reference: Docker docs: Packet filtering and firewalls

stem: The `app` image is distroless (no shell, no curl), and it intermittently can't reach `payments:8443` on a user-defined network. Which two steps are effective for debugging? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run a tools image in app's namespace: `docker run --rm -it --network container:app nicolaka/netshoot`
options.why: You get curl, dig and tcpdump with exactly app's interfaces and DNS.

options.text: Run `docker network inspect` on the network to confirm both containers and their IPs
options.why: It shows whether `payments` is attached and which address it has.

options.text: Run `docker exec app curl payments:8443`
options.why: The distroless image has no curl to execute.

options.text: Recreate both containers with `--link payments` to force resolution
options.why: `--link` is legacy and hides the real problem instead of diagnosing it.

options.text: Restart the Docker daemon to clear the embedded DNS cache
options.why: That disrupts every container and diagnoses nothing.

explanation: Sharing the target container's network stack with `--network container:<name>` is the standard way to debug minimal images: the tools container sees the same interfaces, routes, `/etc/resolv.conf` and embedded DNS. Combine it with `docker network inspect` to verify membership and addresses, then use `dig payments`, `curl -v` and `tcpdump` from inside.

stem: To stop Docker bypassing ufw, an engineer sets `"iptables": false` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restarts the daemon. Which two outcomes should they expect? (Choose two.)

options.text: Containers on bridge networks lose outbound access unless they write replacement rules
options.why: Without Docker's rules there is no masquerading or forwarding for bridges.

options.text: The docs call this inappropriate for most users, because it is likely to break container networking
options.why: The option prevents most rules but isn't a general fix.

options.text: Published ports keep working, now filtered by ufw
options.why: Port publishing relies on the NAT rules Docker no longer creates.

options.text: Docker switches to nftables, which ufw understands
options.why: Turning off iptables doesn't select the nftables backend; that's `firewall-backend`.

options.text: It completely prevents Docker from creating any firewall rules
options.why: The docs say it prevents most rules and that it isn't possible to prevent them all.

explanation: Setting `iptables` (or `ip6tables`) to `false` stops Docker creating most of its rules, but the docs warn it's not appropriate for most users: without replacement rules, bridge containers can't reach the internet, and published ports stop working. It isn't possible to completely prevent Docker from creating firewall rules. Prefer loopback-bound publishing, unpublished internal networks, or `DOCKER-USER` filters.
reference: Docker docs: Packet filtering and firewalls

stem: An app runs in a container on an IPv6-only user-defined network (`docker network create --ipv6 --ipv4=false v6net`), and its config requires an explicit DNS server address. Which value should it use?

options.text: `::1`, the IPv6 loopback, because the container has no IPv4
options.why: Nothing serves DNS on the container's IPv6 loopback.

options.text: The IPv6 address of the network's gateway
options.why: Docker documents no DNS service on the gateway; the embedded server lives elsewhere.

options.text: `fd00::11`, the embedded server's IPv6 counterpart
options.why: There is no IPv6 equivalent of the embedded DNS address.

options.text: `127.0.0.11`, which works even in IPv6-only containers
options.why: The embedded DNS server is only offered at that IPv4 address.

explanation: The embedded DNS server address is `127.0.0.11`, and the docs state there is no IPv6 equivalent: the IPv4 address works even in IPv6-only containers. If an application needs an explicit DNS server, use `127.0.0.11`. It forwards external lookups to the DNS servers configured on the host.
